title: It tells its essence
done: Its idea written for anyone - tables kept as plain text, a guard at the door - and the workings of the step it has reached. It says plainly that it is kept as it is and that its ideas continue in ocoeco.
rejected: Presenting it as where new work goes.

title: tad gets a path of its own
done: tad's backlog and milestones written as tad data and exported through its mark, so the observatory shows how close tad is to being a rhizcut in every repository.
considered: tad as a top tab next to Linux Phones.
rejected: A top tab (it would crowd the overall look); tad as a template (a rhizcut instead).

title: A conditional rule, read right
done: The canon's rule 'when a year of origin is given, an author is required' had been read as 'an author is always required' - tad reported 20 problems where Python's canon passed. The translator now tells a field's own rule from a rule guarded by another field (a dependency), and refuses any other guarded rule. The equivalence proof caught it.

title: Canonical form and checked edits, byte for byte
done: tad canon and tad set, matching DuckDB's own writing exactly: compact JSON, fields in declared order, empty fields as null, rows in their order, new rows at the end. Four proofs passed on the first run.

title: tad check, in Rust, equal to Python's validation
done: A tad crate: declarations as data, translated from the four DuckDB schemas by sqlparser (refusing what it does not know), and every row checked. On the four repositories and eight broken copies it reaches the same verdicts as Python's canon. A first comparison against Python's check misled: that command only compares names; corrected by reading the code.
rejected: That: it does not validate rows; canon does.

title: tad in Rust, designed
done: Looked at what tad is (a 127-line runner and a 478-line renderer, in four repositories, 41 tables using only simple constraints) and at what others built (Frictionless Table Schema, CSV on the Web, Dolt, Datasette). Designed tad in Rust with tables declared as data, proven equal to the Python version before any switch.
rejected: That: a database engine to check text.

title: tad released; the playbook is the first on it
done: tad-v0.1.0 tagged by land --tag on merged code; the conveyor built it for two architectures with checksums and provenance. The playbook moved onto it and its CI went green; tad set made its first real change there (a session entry). Mistakes on the way: an edit check that read '.tad' as a pattern (stopped safely on a false alarm); a commit message predicting document changes that did not happen - corrected in the playbook's own log.

title: Documents rendered by tad, byte for byte
done: The renderer ported to Rust, with Python's string habits (title, capitalize, str) and its look-around patterns (fancy-regex). Every document of the four repositories, both formats, identical to today's Python renderer. Found: three repositories carry older copies of the renderer.
considered: Comparing with each repository's own vendored copy.
rejected: That as the reference: the copies are older; today's engine is the one tad replaces.

title: Every rule of the four tad repositories, as data
done: The 13 cross-table SQL checks became four kinds of declared rule; tad agrees with Python on all four repositories and on seven more broken copies. A test of mine once printed an empty verdict for a declaration I had cut wrongly; tad had refused it rightly - the proof now demands pass, caught, or an error shown.
